paper_title: Thermal aware task assignment for multicore processors using genetic algorithm

extraction.paper_title: Thermal aware task assignment for multicore processors using genetic algorithm

scenario.figure_or_table: Figure 9 and Figure 10 (Section 5.3.2, different initial temperature case); task parameters from Table 1 (PDF page 8)
scenario.description: Thermal-aware GA task assignment on a quad-core CPU. The 20 benchmark tasks are re-assigned to cores each hyper-period according to current core temperatures, and per-core temperatures are simulated with HotSpot (RC thermal model). The paper reports per-core temperature traces (Figure 9) and the maximum inter-core temperature difference per hyper-period (Figure 10, about 8 C after the first hyper-period). The paper publishes no floorplan geometry (no block x, y, width or height), so no complete 2D steady-state experiment is identifiable from the paper alone.
scenario.architecture: Quad-core out-of-order (O3) CPU, 32 KB I-cache and D-cache, dedicated 1 MB L2, 64 MB RAM with DDRx1 memory controller, 2 GHz clock (PDF page 7, Section 5.1, Figure 6 on page 8). Simulators: gem5 for execution time, McPAT for power, HotSpot for temperature.
scenario.workload: 20 independent periodic non-real-time tasks from SPEC2006, MiBench and MediaBench (Table 1, PDF page 8), scheduled with EDF, assigned by the proposed genetic-algorithm task assignment, run for 10 hyper-periods.
scenario.operating_point: Initial core temperatures Core1 65.48 C, Core2 49.77 C, Core3 45.82 C, Core4 51.86 C; ambient 45 C; the final temperature of each hyper-period becomes the initial temperature of the next; simulated time about 14 s.

original_setup.solver: HotSpot compact RC thermal simulator for per-core transient temperatures, fed by gem5 execution times and McPAT task power (PDF pages 4, 7, 10). The paper also gives a lumped single-RC task temperature model (Eqs. 1-2, PDF page 3).
original_setup.optimizer: Genetic algorithm with binary chromosomes (one gene per task), tournament selection, single-point crossover, bitwise mutation and (mu+lambda) survivor selection. It matches each core's assigned task energy to a_j*En_total (Eq. 13, Algorithm 1, PDF pages 6-7).
original_setup.controller: Temperature-driven task-assignment loop. Decision factors a_j are computed from current core temperatures (Eqs. 10-12). The GA assigns tasks to cores each hyper-period under EDF scheduling, and the final HotSpot temperatures feed the next hyper-period (PDF pages 5-7). This is not a DVFS or closed-loop cooling controller.
original_setup.benchmark: 20 independent periodic non-real-time tasks from SPEC2006, MiBench and MediaBench (Table 1, PDF page 8). Scenario: quad-core O3 CPU, 2 GHz, 10 hyper-periods, different-initial-temperature case with Core1 65.48 C, Core2 49.77 C, Core3 45.82 C, Core4 51.86 C and ambient 45 C (Section 5.3.2, PDF page 10).

thermal_observable.location: Maximum temperature difference between the cores of the quad-core CPU. The value is read approximately from Figure 10 and stated as about 8 C in the text and conclusion.
thermal_observable.aggregation: Per-hyper-period maximum inter-core temperature difference over 10 hyper-periods, about 8 C except for the first hyper-period. It is a transient HotSpot result over roughly 14 s of simulation, not a steady-state peak. The figure value is approximate and uncertain.

physical_mismatches.reason: The paper publishes no floorplan geometry (block x, y, width, height), so no complete spatial experiment can be reconstructed. Any 2D placement would be separate, illustrative and generated by the runner.

The paper's observable is a transient, time-varying inter-core temperature difference over hyper-periods with task-switching power. A steady-state 2D solve with a one-row power trace cannot reproduce it, and the temperatures cannot be compared numerically.

Power is published per task (leakage plus dynamic watts, Table 1) rather than per block, and there is no published rule for splitting it across cores or blocks. Task-to-core mapping per hyper-period is not published.

The controller (temperature-based decision factors, EDF scheduling, hyper-period feedback) and the genetic-algorithm optimizer are not part of a static thermal Studio solve and cannot be replicated there.

Package, heat spreader, heat sink, cooling and HotSpot RC parameters are not reported. The quad-core CPU is a monolithic die with caches, not a 3D or interposer chiplet system, so Ascend910 or ATPlace2.5D style scenarios do not apply.
Reliability is only motivated qualitatively in the introduction (lifetime halved per 10-15 C). No reliability metric is computed.

methods.note: The text on pages 3-7 supports the GA task assignment, Eqs. 10-13, the HotSpot-fed hyper-period loop, and the gem5/McPAT/HotSpot toolchain. Page 3 supports the lumped RC model. The extraction wrongly cites page 4 and page 10 for HotSpot, and it does not flag that EDF is combined with tasks the paper calls non-real-time (page 4). The abstract's 8 C figure is stated as a maximum, but the first hyper-period is excluded.

config.note: There is no HotSpot floorplan or config, gem5/McPAT config files, or pinned assets. data.note: The text values (initial temperatures, 45 C ambient, 2 GHz, 10 hyper-periods, about 14 s, 4 cores) match pages 7-10. Table 1 gives per-task power with no per-block or per-core mapping. Figures 9 and 10 exist only as pdftotext output, so no figure was visually verified or digitized, and no numeric trace data is supplied. The 8 C observable rests only on the text 'slightly 8 C'.

HotSpot is cited to PDF pages 4, 7 and 10, but pages 4 and 10 only mention gem5 and McPAT (page 10 only in the conclusion). HotSpot appears on pages 1, 5 and 7.

The paper gives 8 C in the abstract and conclusion, but 'nearly 9 C' for the equal-initial case (page 9). The 8 C figure holds only after the first hyper-period (page 10). Without the figure data, which value corresponds to the selected scenario is not verified.

The extraction pairs 'non-real-time' tasks with EDF scheduling without noting the paper's inconsistency. Section 3.2 says non-real-time tasks, while the abstract claims no deadlines are lost under EDF. No task deadlines or periods are published.

assessment.summary: The 2D screening label is not_2d_applicable and Studio did not run (simulation status skipped; simulation_allowed=false). The selected scenario is the thermal-aware GA task assignment on a quad-core O3 CPU (Section 5.3.2, Figures 9 and 10), classed as a custom_2d_steady experiment with an empty floorplan and empty power_w. The gate failed on input validity: a custom experiment needs 1-128 blocks and a power_w object. Further blocking facts: evidence items 11 and 13 lack a valid page or pinned asset locator, there is no cited paper thermal observable or steady/transient regime in the gate's view, there is no linked artifact, and the adversarial and independent reviews are unresolved. Both input_gate_pass and scientific_gate_pass are false, independently_verified is false, and comparison_valid is false. Because Studio did not run, there is no Studio temperature, no transient trace (a custom steady run would not have one anyway), and no input.flp or input.ptrace. This is not a bundled EV6/GCC adapted demonstration, and no pinned Ascend910 or ATPlace source commit or generated-placement assumption applies, because the CPU is a monolithic quad-core die with caches and not a chiplet system. The paper's observable is about 8 C, the maximum inter-core temperature difference per hyper-period over 10 hyper-periods (about 14 s of HotSpot transient simulation, excluding the first hyper-period). It is read approximately from Figure 10 and the text and is not digitized. The initial core temperatures (65.48, 49.77, 45.82 and 51.86 C) and the 45 C ambient are initial and boundary conditions, not power or geometry inputs. No numerical comparison is possible. Only qualitative reasoning is defensible: thermal-aware reassignment of tasks that balances per-core energy should narrow inter-core temperature spread over time. Studio was not used to test this, and nothing here replicates the paper's result. The text also gives about 9 C for the equal-initial case, which conflicts with the 8 C cited in the abstract and conclusion.
